payload.title: HTTP4-over-WebTransport Protocol Sandbox — Proposal
payload.body: Engineering proposal for an experimental, receiver-driven "HTTP4" transport: a browser JavaScript client and a Go server over WebTransport datagrams, with the receiver pacing delivery via SRPT-scheduled GRANTs (after Stanford's Homa). Recorded as submitted on 2026-09-22. Section 4 refers to client and server code that was not included in the submission.

blocks.text:
## 1. Executive Summary

Modern web transport protocols (HTTP/3, QUIC) remain sender-driven, utilizing congestion windows (CUBIC/BBR) that allocate network capacity based on fair sharing. Under heavy or unbalanced loads, this results in queue bloat and high tail latencies.

This project aims to implement a functional user-space proof-of-concept for HTTP4, an internet-scale adaptation of Stanford's data-center Homa protocol. By utilizing WebTransport, we will invert network control, allowing the receiver to pace data delivery via explicit Grants scheduled by Shortest Remaining Processing Time (SRPT).

## 2. System Architecture Overview

The sandbox relies on a split-stack implementation. The client handles rendering priority, stream tracking, and grant issuance. The server serves as a compliant, passive data repository that releases bytes only upon structural validation of receiver-driven tokens.

```
┌──────────────────────────────┐              ┌──────────────────────────────┐
│    Web Browser (JS Client)   │              │     Go Backend Server        │
│                              │              │                              │
│  ┌────────────────────────┐  │              │  ┌────────────────────────┐  │
│  │   UI Rendering Stack   │  │              │  │  Static Resource Pool  │  │
│  └───────────┬────────────┘  │              │  └───────────▲────────────┘  │
│              │ (Priority)    │              │              │ (Byte Slices) │
│  ┌───────────▼────────────┐  │ WebTransport │  ┌───────────┴────────────┐  │
│  │  SRPT Grant Scheduler  ├──┼─► Datagrams ─┼─►│ Passive Sender Engine  │  │
│  └────────────────────────┘  │  (UDP 443)   │  └────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────┘              └──────────────────────────────┘
```

### Protocol Interaction Lifecycle

1. **Unscheduled Initiation:** The client sends an un-granted, unscheduled Datagram requesting an asset ID.
2. **Metadata Priming:** The server replies with Packet 0 containing the total payload dimensions.
3. **Paced Evaluation:** The client inserts the transaction into its local SRPT map, calculates weight modifications (based on asset type or viewport visibility), and emits GRANT datagrams.
4. **Passive Emission:** The server pushes packet offsets exactly matching the granted ceiling.

## 3. Wire Format Specification (HTTP4 Datagram Frame)

To maximize throughput, all control and data packets are encapsulated directly into WebTransport Datagrams (restricted to an MTU boundary of 1200 bytes).

### Plaintext Common Header (All Packets)

- Byte 0: Packet Type (0x01: REQ, 0x02: DATA, 0x03: GRANT, 0x04: RESEND)
- Bytes 1-8: RPC_ID (64-bit cryptographic identifier matching Request/Response pairs)

### Payload Layouts (Post-Header Encapsulation)

**0x02: DATA (Server ➔ Client)**

| Total Size (4 Bytes) | Chunk Offset (4 Bytes) | Encrypted Byte Stream |
|---|---|---|

**0x03: GRANT (Client ➔ Server)**

| Max Offset (4 Bytes) | Priority Class (1B) |
|---|---|

**0x04: RESEND (Client ➔ Server)**

| Missing Start (4 Bytes) | Missing End (4 Bytes) |
|---|---|

## 4. Engineering Implementation Blueprints

Here is the initial software architecture drafted for the sandbox engine.

**Client Implementation (Browser JavaScript):** This script initializes the WebTransport connection, processes raw packet frames, evaluates remaining processing time, and handles rendering priority hooks.

**Server Implementation (Go Engine):** This backend infrastructure runs concurrently using Goroutines, monitoring consumer-driven GRANT updates without generating blocking buffer overhead.

_(The code referred to here was not included in the submitted proposal.)_

## 5. Project Roadmap & Success Benchmarks

```
┌────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────┐      ┌────────────────────────┐
│ Phase 1: Local Loop    │ ───► │ Phase 2: WAN Injection │ ───► │ Phase 3: Starvation Fix│
│ Datagram verification  │      │ Apply artificial loss  │      │ Age weight adjustments │
└────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────┘      └────────────────────────┘
```

To evaluate the validity of this architecture against native HTTP/3, testing will be executed across three evaluation goals:

- **Success Metric 1 (Tail Latency Minimization):** Under asymmetric multi-asset transfers, the 99th percentile recovery time for tool-calling API frames must experience an 80%+ decline relative to multiplexed HTTP/3 streams.
- **Success Metric 2 (Head-of-Line Elimination):** Heavy background image loads must not stall or produce structural delays on parallel layout-blocking styles.
- **Success Metric 3 (Pacing Transparency):** Verify through network capture software that the server emits zero un-granted bursts, confirming absolute client-side control over network pipelines.

payload.title: G1 — Local loop delivers every asset intact over the HTTP4 datagram protocol
payload.body: Phase 1 correctness. A fixed set of assets (1 KB – 50 MB) requested via REQ → Packet 0 → GRANT → DATA (+ RESEND) on a local WebTransport session must reassemble byte-for-byte. Measured as % of assets in the integrity suite whose SHA-256 matches the source.

payload.title: G2 — Server emits zero un-granted bytes (pacing transparency)
payload.body: Proposal Success Metric 3. The server must never send DATA past the highest granted offset for an RPC (beyond the agreed unscheduled Packet 0). Measured server-side: a counter of bytes sent beyond the grant ceiling, summed over a test run. A packet capture cannot show this because QUIC encrypts every datagram; use server counters or qlog.

payload.title: G3 — p99 latency of small API responses under mixed load drops ≥80% vs HTTP/3
payload.body: Proposal Success Metric 1. Workload: small (≤4 KB) API-style responses competing with large asset transfers. Metric: % reduction in p99 completion time for the small responses, HTTP4 vs multiplexed HTTP/3 streams, same hosts and network conditions. Note: WebTransport datagrams remain subject to QUIC's own congestion control, so this measures receiver-side SRPT scheduling on top of QUIC, not a replacement for it.

payload.title: G4 — Heavy image loads do not delay layout-blocking styles
payload.body: Proposal Success Metric 2. Metric: % increase in stylesheet completion time when a large background image transfer runs in parallel, vs the same stylesheet loaded alone. Target not yet set — see the open question on the allowed slowdown.

payload.title: G5 — Correctness and pacing hold under WAN loss and delay
payload.body: Phase 2. Metric: % of cells in the impairment matrix (loss 0/1/5% × RTT 0/50/150 ms) where G1 and G2 both hold.

payload.title: G6 — Large transfers are never starved by SRPT
payload.body: Phase 3. Under a sustained stream of small requests, the worst-case slowdown of a large transfer (completion time ÷ its completion time with no competition). Target not yet set — see the open question on the starvation bound.

payload.title: What slowdown of stylesheet loads is acceptable while a large image downloads (G4 target)?
payload.body: The proposal says heavy image loads 'must not stall or produce structural delays' on layout-blocking styles, but gives no number. G4 measures the % increase in stylesheet completion time with a parallel large image vs alone. With QUIC congestion control still underneath, 0% is not physically achievable; some contention is unavoidable.

options.consequence: Strict; demonstrates near-complete isolation. Likely needs priority classes to preempt the image aggressively.
Moderate; clearly better than typical HTTP/3 contention while leaving room for QUIC-level effects.

options.option: Relative: ≥X% better than the HTTP/3 baseline
options.consequence: Measures improvement rather than an absolute bound; requires the HTTP/3 baseline harness before G4 can be scored.

payload.title: What worst-case slowdown for large transfers counts as 'not starved' (G6 target)?
payload.body: Pure SRPT can starve a large transfer indefinitely while small requests keep arriving. Phase 3 adds age-based weight adjustments. G6 needs a bound on completion time ÷ uncontended completion time for a large transfer under sustained small-request load.

options.consequence: Tight fairness; aging must kick in early, which erodes some of G3's tail-latency win.
Balanced; small requests keep strong priority but large ones are guaranteed to finish.
Favours G3 heavily; only prevents true starvation.

payload.title: Phase 1: Local loop — datagram protocol working end to end on localhost
payload.body: Parent for Phase 1 of the HTTP4 sandbox (doc-sjj28a2). Done when the integrity suite scores G1 = 100% and G2 = 0 un-granted bytes on a localhost WebTransport session.

payload.title: Scaffold repo: Go server module, static JS client, and localhost WebTransport TLS setup
payload.body:
Create `server/` (Go module using quic-go + webtransport-go) and `client/` (plain ES modules served statically). Generate a dev certificate that Chrome accepts for WebTransport on localhost: either a self-signed ECDSA P-256 cert valid ≤14 days passed via `serverCertificateHashes`, or a locally trusted CA (mkcert). Add a script that regenerates the cert and prints its SHA-256 hash for the client.

Acceptance: the browser opens a WebTransport session to the Go server on localhost and one echo datagram goes each way.

payload.title: Specify and implement the HTTP4 datagram codec in Go and JS with shared test vectors
payload.body:
Implement encode/decode for REQ, DATA, GRANT, and RESEND per doc-sjj28a2 §3 (1-byte type + 8-byte RPC_ID header; big-endian fields). Write a spec at `docs/wire-format.md` that fills the gaps the proposal leaves:
- **REQ payload** is not defined: specify how the asset ID is encoded (e.g. a 2-byte length plus UTF-8 path).
- **Packet 0**: define it as a DATA packet at offset 0 carrying Total Size and the first unscheduled bytes, and fix how many unscheduled bytes the server may send before any GRANT. G2 depends on this number.
- **RPC_ID**: the client generates it as 8 random bytes via `crypto.getRandomValues`.
- **Payload sizing**: data per packet = `maxDatagramSize` − 17. Use the negotiated size, never a hard-coded 1200.
- **Encryption**: drop the extra "Encrypted Byte Stream" layer, because QUIC already encrypts datagrams, and record that as a decision.

Acceptance: golden hex vectors in `testdata/wire/` round-trip identically through both the Go and JS codecs, including a malformed/truncated input set that must be rejected.

payload.title: Build the asset fixture set for the integrity suite
payload.body:
Create a deterministic set of test assets for the server's static resource pool: 1 KB, 4 KB, 64 KB, 1 MB, 10 MB, and 50 MB, plus edge sizes (0 bytes, exactly one payload, one payload + 1 byte). Generate them from a seeded PRNG rather than checking large files in, and emit a manifest of SHA-256 hashes.

Acceptance: `scripts/gen-fixtures` reproduces identical files and manifest on every run.

payload.title: Server passive sender: answer REQ with Packet 0 and send DATA only up to the granted offset
payload.body:
In the Go server, keep per-RPC state (asset, total size, grant ceiling, next offset) keyed by RPC_ID. On REQ: look up the asset, send Packet 0 plus at most the unscheduled allowance from the wire spec. On GRANT: raise the ceiling (ignore any grant that lowers it) and send DATA up to it. Use one goroutine per session, and never block the datagram receive loop on sending.

Instrument for G2: count bytes per RPC sent past ceiling + unscheduled allowance, and expose the totals (metrics endpoint or JSON on shutdown). The counter must be checked at the send path itself, not inferred afterwards.

Acceptance: unit tests with a fake transport show zero sends past the ceiling for grants that arrive out of order, repeat, or are missing. Unknown asset IDs and unknown RPC_IDs are handled without panicking.

payload.title: JS client: request assets, reassemble DATA, and issue grants from a basic SRPT scheduler
payload.body:
In the browser client: open the session, read `transport.datagrams.maxDatagramSize`, and send REQ. On Packet 0, add the RPC to an SRPT map keyed by remaining bytes. Keep a fixed grant window (e.g. a set number of bytes in flight) and give it to the RPC with the fewest remaining bytes first. Reassemble into a preallocated buffer and track which byte ranges have arrived. Resolve a promise with the bytes when complete.

Phase 1 uses size only for scheduling. Priority classes and viewport weighting come later, but GRANT should already carry the priority byte.

Acceptance: fetching a single asset and several concurrent assets both return correct bytes on a lossless localhost link, and an instrumented run shows the smallest remaining RPC is always granted first.

payload.title: Recover lost datagrams with RESEND: client gap detection and server retransmit
payload.body:
Datagrams are unreliable even on localhost, because they are dropped when buffers fill. Client: when bytes below the grant ceiling haven't arrived within a timeout (based on the measured RTT, with a floor), send RESEND for each missing range, with backoff and a retry limit. Server: on RESEND, resend exactly the missing range, capped at the grant ceiling. A resend of granted bytes is not an un-granted byte, and the G2 counter must not count it.

Also handle a lost REQ or Packet 0: the client resends REQ with the same RPC_ID if Packet 0 doesn't arrive in time, and the server answers repeat REQs without creating a second RPC.

Acceptance: with a test hook that drops a chosen set of datagrams (every Nth, a Packet 0, the final chunk), every transfer still completes with the correct hash.

payload.title: Automated Phase 1 integrity suite in headless Chrome that reports G1 and G2
payload.body:
Write a script (Playwright + headless Chromium) that starts the Go server with the fixture pool and loads the client. It fetches every fixture one at a time and then all at once, and compares SHA-256 hashes against the manifest. At the end it reads the server's un-granted byte counter and prints both figures as JSON: `{ "g1_pct_intact": …, "g2_ungranted_bytes": … }`. Run it once with no drops and once with the RESEND drop hook enabled.

Acceptance: one command runs the whole suite with a non-zero exit on failure. Its output is the evidence for recording measurements against G1 and G2 and closing Phase 1.

payload.title: Project layout: server/ (Go module) + client/ (browser) with shared testdata/, docs/, scripts/, tests/ at root
payload.body: Chosen by the user while scaffolding iss-ajda0b4. The Go module lives in server/ with cmd/http4d and internal/. The browser client lives in client/. Wire vectors, assets, and the spec are shared at the repo root, and a root package.json holds dev dependencies only. This matches the `touches` paths already recorded on the Phase 1 issues. Rejected: B, Go module at repo root with web/ (more idiomatic `go test ./...`, but the issue paths would need changing); C, spec/ plus impl/go and impl/js (more structure than a two-implementation sandbox needs).

payload.title: Dev TLS: server generates an in-memory self-signed ECDSA cert at startup and serves its SHA-256 for serverCertificateHashes
payload.body: Chosen by the user while scaffolding iss-ajda0b4. At each start the server creates a P-256 cert valid for less than 14 days, as serverCertificateHashes requires, and exposes the hash on the same origin that serves the page. With no files on disk and no manual renewal, expiry never breaks local runs. This replaces the 'regenerate cert script' named in the issue. Rejected: cert files plus a scripts/devcert regenerator (has to be re-run every 14 days or fewer); mkcert (not installed, and it modifies the system trust store).

payload.title: Client is written in TypeScript and bundled with a one-shot esbuild build to client/dist
payload.body: Chosen by the user while scaffolding iss-ajda0b4. Full TypeScript, with tsc --noEmit for type checking and esbuild for bundling. There is no watch mode or dev server; the user's standing rule is 'never run dev task'. Rejected: JS with JSDoc and tsc --checkJs (no build step, but weaker types); plain JS.

payload.title: Browser acceptance checks run as one-shot headless tests that start the server, drive Chromium, and exit
payload.body: Chosen by the user while scaffolding iss-ajda0b4. The user's standing rule is 'never run dev task', so agents never leave a long-lived dev server running. Browser verification is a one-shot test process that owns the server's whole lifecycle. Rejected: the user runs the server by hand; a Go-only WebTransport client check with the browser deferred.

payload.title: Chrome 153 reports WebTransport maxDatagramSize = 1024 bytes on a localhost session, below the proposal's 1200-byte assumption
payload.body: Measured by the scaffold echo test: Google Chrome 153.0.8010.53, headless, macOS arm64, against the quic-go v0.63 / webtransport-go v0.13 server on 127.0.0.1, with `transport.datagrams.maxDatagramSize` read after `ready`. Result 1024. With the 17-byte DATA header (9 common + 8), that leaves at most 1007 payload bytes per datagram, not ~1183. This is one browser and version on loopback; other paths and browsers may report different values, so codec sizing must use the negotiated value at runtime.

sources.note: Output of `npm run test:echo`: {"ok":true,"attempts":1,"rttMs":1,"maxDatagramSize":1024}
§3 assumes 'an MTU boundary of 1200 bytes'

payload.title: Headless Chrome loads the client from the Go server, opens a WebTransport session trusted only via serverCertificateHashes, sends one datagram, and receives the identical datagram back. The test starts and stops the server itself, and no process is left running.

payload.evidence: `npm run test:echo` on 2026-09-22 (Chrome 153.0.8010.53, Go 1.27.1, Node 24.14.1) → ✔ 1/1, echo {"ok":true,"attempts":1,"rttMs":1,"maxDatagramSize":1024}; `pgrep http4d` found no process afterwards. To re-check: `npm install && npm test`.

payload.evidence: `cd server && go vet ./... && go test -count=1 ./...` on 2026-09-22 → ok internal/devcert, ok internal/server.

payload.title: Unscheduled bytes are client-authorized: REQ carries initial_grant, and the server treats it as a GRANT for [0, initial_grant)
payload.body:
Resolves the 'Packet 0 / unscheduled allowance' gap named in iss-2atv8th. Homa lets a sender push a fixed amount of unscheduled data (about one RTT's worth) before any grant. Here the client names that amount itself in a u32 field on REQ. The server never sends a byte the client did not authorize, so G2 is a strict zero with no exemption for a first burst, and the client can still ask for Homa-style unscheduled bytes by setting initial_grant to about one BDP. Packet 0 is always the DATA packet at offset 0 and is sent even when initial_grant = 0, with an empty payload that only delivers total_size.

Rejected: a server-side constant allowance U. It creates a G2 exemption that the server has to account for, and the receiver cannot tune it per request (e.g. 0 for below-the-fold images).

payload.title: Add ERROR packet type 0x05 (NOT_FOUND, BAD_REQUEST, UNKNOWN_RPC) to the wire format
payload.body: The proposal defines no failure signal. Without one, a REQ for an unknown asset, or a GRANT or RESEND for an RPC the server has forgotten, gets no answer, and the client can only time out. ERROR is 10 bytes (header plus a 1-byte code) and ends the RPC. Decoders accept unknown codes so that codes can be added later without breaking older decoders. Rejected: silently dropping such packets (the client can't tell loss from failure, which inflates tail latency); overloading DATA with a sentinel total_size (ambiguous for empty assets).

payload.title: No application-layer encryption: the DATA payload is plaintext asset bytes inside QUIC's encryption
payload.body: The proposal's DATA layout says 'Encrypted Byte Stream' and its header 'Plaintext'. Every WebTransport datagram is already encrypted and authenticated by QUIC (TLS 1.3), so a second layer adds CPU cost and key management and protects nothing more. The rpc_id is random for collision avoidance, not secrecy. Rejected: per-RPC AEAD over the payload.

payload.title: All 10 hand-written valid vectors in testdata/wire/vectors.json decode to the expected packet and re-encode to identical hex, in both the Go and TS codecs; all 20 invalid vectors are rejected by both.

Client: when bytes below the grant ceiling haven't arrived within a timeout (based on the measured RTT, with a floor), send RESEND for each missing range, with backoff and a retry limit. payload.title: Datagram size limits differ by direction: Chrome 153 accepts 1200-byte datagrams from the server while reporting maxDatagramSize = 1024 for its own sends
payload.body: Browser fetch test on localhost, 2026-09-22: the quic-go server (initial max datagram 1200, so 1183-byte DATA payloads) sent 3,708 DATA packets carrying 4,352,224 bytes to headless Chrome 153. It got 0 DatagramTooLargeError (chunk_shrinks = 0), and Chrome received and decoded every packet (client packetsIn 3,709, 0 malformed). `maxDatagramSize` therefore limits only what the browser sends (REQ/GRANT/RESEND, all small), not what it receives. The server's limit comes from quic-go's own estimate and the peer's max_datagram_frame_size, and the server shrinks its chunk if QUIC refuses a size. Loopback only; real paths may have a smaller PMTU.

sources.note: tests/fetch/fetch.test.ts output: server {data_packets:3708, data_bytes:4352224, chunk_shrinks:0}; client {packetsIn:3709, malformedIn:0}
Earlier finding: maxDatagramSize = 1024. This one refines it: that limit is send-side only.

payload.title: Recover from loss without waiting for a full stall: gap-triggered early RESEND and RTT samples beyond the REQ
payload.body:
Found while verifying iss-dfchynh. Recovery is correct but slow under heavy loss. With the server dropping every 7th DATA, the 8-asset concurrent batch takes ~600 ms against ~25 ms lossless (5% random loss: ~180 ms). The client only RESENDs once a transfer has made no progress for a full RTO (20 ms floor). Missing bytes still count against the 128 KiB grant budget, so holes fill the budget, the transfer stalls, and each round costs one timeout.

Proposed:
1. **Early RESEND:** when DATA arrives more than a reordering threshold (e.g. 3 packets' worth) past a gap, RESEND that gap right away, like TCP's duplicate-ACK fast retransmit. Keep the timer as the fallback. Don't RESEND the same gap again within one RTT.
2. **RTT samples beyond the REQ:** currently the only sample is REQ→first DATA, and Karn's rule discards it when the REQ was retransmitted. In the 'client drops each first REQ' scenario srtt was never set, so the RTO stayed at the 100 ms default. Also sample GRANT→first byte past the previous grant, and RESEND→first resent byte, when unambiguous.

Acceptance: in tests/loss, the every=7 concurrent batch finishes within 3× the lossless time with 0 extra duplicate bytes when there is no loss. srtt is set in every scenario.

payload.title: Phase 1 integrity suite: payload bytes sent past a grant (server counter, both passes)
payload.body: Same `npm run integrity` run as the G1 measurement (2026-09-22T13:14:44Z). Sum of `ungranted_bytes_sent` from the server's /metrics.json after each pass (clean 0 + lossy 0). The server checks the counter at its single DATA send path (server/internal/sender), not a packet capture, because QUIC encrypts datagrams. Separately, the Go tests check every DATA packet against an independent client-side grant oracle.

payload.title: G7 — Drop-in library: build a demo site that runs on HTTP4 without writing any protocol code
payload.body:
Requested by the user on 2026-09-22: "build drop in library to allow me to create a site that uses this protocol as a demo". The goal is a site author's experience: take an ordinary site (HTML, CSS, JS, images, API calls), add the HTTP4 client and server libraries, and have its subresources load over HTTP4, falling back to normal HTTP where WebTransport is unavailable.

Metric: % of the demo site's same-origin subresource bytes delivered over HTTP4 on a WebTransport-capable browser, with the site containing no protocol code of its own (it uses only the libraries' public APIs). Target 100.

payload.title: Phase 2: WAN injection — correctness and pacing hold under delay, jitter and loss
payload.body:
Parent for Phase 2 of doc-sjj28a2 ("Apply artificial loss"). Phase 1 proved correctness on loopback with loss injected only inside the sender. Phase 2 puts a real impaired path between Chrome and the server (delay, jitter, reordering, loss in both directions, at the UDP layer under QUIC) and scores G5 over the matrix loss {0, 1, 5}% × RTT {0, 50, 150} ms.

Done when the matrix runner reports G5 = 100%, i.e. G1 = 100% and G2 = 0 in every cell within its deadline.

payload.title: Benchmark: HTTP4 vs HTTP/3 in the same browser, workloads and conditions (G3, G4)
payload.body:
Parent for the proposal's comparison claims. Success Metric 1 (G3: p99 latency of small API responses under mixed load, ≥80% lower than HTTP/3) and Success Metric 2 (G4: heavy images don't delay layout-blocking styles) both need a fair HTTP/3 baseline. The baseline is the same Chrome, same machine, same assets, same impairment, with the same bytes fetched over multiplexed HTTP/3 streams, and a harness that runs both stacks through identical workloads.

Done when G3 and G4 each have a recorded measurement from this harness, on clean loopback and at least the Phase 2 matrix cells (1%, 50 ms) and (0%, 150 ms).

payload.title: Drop-in library for sites: HTTP4 client and server packages plus a demo site (G7)
payload.body:
Parent for G7. Turn the sandbox's client (client/src) and server (server/internal) into libraries a site author can adopt without touching protocol code, then prove it with a demo site built only on their public APIs.

How a site integrates the client (transparent Service Worker, explicit JS API, or declarative HTML attributes) and how the server is packaged is an open question for the user. The integration-specific issues below are blocked on it.

payload.title: UDP impairment proxy: add delay, jitter, reordering and loss between Chrome and the server, no root needed
payload.body:
A user-space Go program (server/cmd/impair) that sits on a UDP port in front of http4d's WebTransport port and forwards datagrams both ways. It applies configurable one-way delay, jitter, reordering, random and burst loss, and optionally a bandwidth cap, separately per direction and deterministically from a seed. The page's config.json advertises the proxy's port, so Chrome's QUIC connection runs end to end through it. serverCertificateHashes still works, because it pins the certificate, not the address.

Why not dummynet/pfctl or tc: those need root, differ between macOS and Linux, and are awkward to run inside a one-shot test. A proxy impairs every UDP packet QUIC sends, including ACKs and handshake packets, which the sender's -drop hook cannot.

Acceptance: Go tests measure the proxy itself. RTT is added within ±2 ms of the configured value, the loss rate is within binomial tolerance, and the same seed reproduces the same drop pattern. A browser test fetches through the proxy at 50 ms RTT and 1% loss and every asset arrives intact.

payload.title: Size the grant budget and initial grant from measured RTT (bandwidth-delay product) instead of fixed 128 KiB / 4 packets
payload.body:
With a fixed 128 KiB budget, throughput is capped at budget ÷ RTT. That is ~0.85 MB/s at 150 ms, so the 50 MiB fixture alone would take ~60 s and blow the Phase 2 deadlines. Homa sizes its unscheduled bytes and grant overcommitment from RTTbytes (the bandwidth-delay product).

Proposed:
- Budget = max(floor, k × estimated BDP), with BDP from srtt × a delivery-rate estimate (bytes received per RTT). Cap it, so Chrome's incoming datagram queue (incomingHighWaterMark) and QUIC's own flow control aren't overrun.
- initial_grant ≈ one BDP, capped. Keep 4 packets until an RTT sample exists.

Note: QUIC's congestion controller still paces the server underneath (proposal caveat under G3), so the budget should keep enough in flight not to starve it. It should not try to replace it.

Acceptance: through the impairment proxy at 150 ms RTT on a clean path, 50 MiB completes within 2× its HTTP/3 time. At 0 ms, lossless performance does not regress vs Phase 1 (`npm run integrity` timings).

payload.title: Phase 2 matrix runner: integrity suite across loss {0,1,5}% × RTT {0,50,150} ms, reporting G5
payload.body:
Extend tests/integrity (or add tests/matrix) to run the fixture pool through the impairment proxy in each of the 9 cells: single fetches and then concurrent ones, SHA-256 against the manifest, and the server's un-granted counter. The per-cell deadline scales with RTT. Output: JSON with per-cell G1/G2, timings, recoveries and duplicate bytes, plus g5_pct_cells_passing. Exit 1 unless every cell passes.

Loss applies in both directions at the proxy. The existing server -drop hook stays available as an extra rule but isn't the Phase 2 loss model.

Acceptance: one command (e.g. `npm run matrix`) produces the JSON. Its first run gets recorded as a G5 measurement even if it fails; failing cells become issues.

payload.title: HTTP/3 baseline: serve the same assets over plain HTTP/3 and make headless Chrome use it
payload.body:
Add an HTTP/3 file server (quic-go http3) to http4d, serving the same asset directory from the same process and certificate, on its own UDP port. The benchmark page fetches the same assets with fetch() over multiplexed HTTP/3 streams.

Catch: serverCertificateHashes only applies to WebTransport. For ordinary fetch() over HTTP/3 against a self-signed certificate, Chrome must be launched with `--origin-to-force-quic-on=127.0.0.1:<port>` and `--ignore-certificate-errors-spki-list=<base64 SHA-256 of the cert's SPKI>`. The server exposes that SPKI hash, and the test harness passes both flags. Verify that the protocol really is h3: `performance.getEntries()` nextHopProtocol === "h3". Fail the benchmark if it isn't, because a silent fallback to HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 over TCP would make any comparison meaningless.

Fairness: the baseline uses Chrome's default HTTP/3 prioritisation. Also record a stronger variant where API calls use `fetch(..., {priority: "high"})`, so G3 can't be won against a strawman.

Acceptance: a test fetches every fixture over h3 (nextHopProtocol verified) with the correct SHA-256, through the impairment proxy as well once that exists.

payload.title: G3 benchmark: p99 of small API responses under concurrent large downloads, HTTP4 vs HTTP/3
payload.body:
Workload (proposal Success Metric 1, 'tool-calling API frames' taken as small API responses):
- Background: 4 concurrent large downloads (10 MiB each), restarted as they finish, so the link stays loaded.
- Foreground: API calls for 1–4 KiB responses, arriving as a Poisson process at ~50/s, for enough time to collect ≥ 2,000 samples per run (p99 needs well over 100 tail samples).
- The same schedule, from a seeded generator, runs over HTTP4 and over HTTP/3 (default and priority:"high" variants, see iss-0sjtwnx).
- Metric: per-call completion time (request issued → full body available). Report p50/p90/p99/p99.9 for each stack and the G3 value = 100 × (1 − p99_HTTP4 ÷ p99_HTTP3), against the stronger baseline variant.

Conditions: clean loopback first. Then, through the impairment proxy (iss-x4fs0fm), at (1%, 50 ms) and (0%, 150 ms).

Acceptance: `npm run bench:g3` prints the JSON above and it gets recorded as a G3 measurement. Five repeated runs show a spread small enough to trust the p99 (report it).

payload.title: G4 benchmark: stylesheet completion time alone vs with a large image downloading in parallel, HTTP4 vs HTTP/3
payload.body:
Workload (proposal Success Metric 2): a ~20–60 KB layout-blocking stylesheet, fetched alone and then while a large image (e.g. 10 MiB) is already downloading. Many repetitions per stack, the same schedule for HTTP4 and HTTP/3. Metric (G4): % increase in stylesheet completion time with the image vs without, per stack. Both are reported, so the target question (que-hzwqhs8: absolute bound vs improvement over HTTP/3) can be scored either way.

A real page-load variant (link rel=stylesheet plus a large img, timing first render) belongs with the drop-in library demo, once its integration style is chosen.

Acceptance: `npm run bench:g4` prints both stacks' slowdowns, on clean loopback and at (1%, 50 ms) through the proxy. The result is recorded as a G4 measurement.

payload.title: Protocol: carry response metadata (Content-Type, length, validators) so browsers can use HTTP4 bodies as real resources
payload.body:
HTTP4 v0 delivers only bytes plus total_size. A drop-in integration has to hand the browser real Responses. Scripts and stylesheets are subject to strict MIME checking (a module script without a JavaScript Content-Type is refused), images and fonts need correct types, and caching needs ETag/Last-Modified.

Options:
1. **Metadata block in Packet 0:** a length-prefixed header block ahead of the body bytes (wire v1). One round trip, but it complicates offsets.
2. **New META packet type (0x06):** sent before or with Packet 0, retransmitted on a repeated REQ, and allowed without a grant because it is metadata, not body. G2 must define it as not counting toward un-granted bytes.
3. **Client-side guessing from the file extension:** no protocol change, but wrong for extensionless API routes and unacceptable for a general drop-in library.

Recommendation: option 2, with a compact encoding (e.g. QPACK-free, a varint-length list of name/value pairs limited to a small allowlist: content-type, etag, last-modified, cache-control). Update docs/wire-format.md to v1, the vectors, both codecs, sender, client, and add an ERROR→HTTP-status mapping for the Response.

Acceptance: a Response built by the client library for a .js/.css/.png/.json fixture has the server-supplied Content-Type, and a module script and a stylesheet loaded through it are accepted by Chrome.

payload.title: Client library package: a public, documented HTTP4 client API with a Response-returning fetch and automatic fallback
payload.body:
Split the sandbox client into a library with a small public surface, separate from the sandbox page and its test hooks:
- Entry point exporting `connect(url, opts)` / `Http4Client`, and a `fetch(input, init?) → Promise<Response>` that looks like the platform fetch. It maps URL paths to asset IDs and builds Response objects with metadata (from the metadata issue).
- **Fallback:** if WebTransport is missing (feature detection), the session fails, or a transfer errors, fall back to the platform fetch() transparently, and expose which transport served each request.
- Build: ESM bundle + .d.ts, a version, no dependencies. dropOutgoing and trace stay available but documented as test-only.
- Publishing target (npm vs vendored file) can wait. Build it so either works.

Acceptance: a minimal page that imports only the package's public entry fetches the fixture pool over HTTP4. The same page in a browser without WebTransport (simulated by deleting window.WebTransport) still loads everything via fallback, and the API reports it.

payload.title: Server packaging: make the HTTP4 sender usable outside this repo (public Go package and/or a `serve <dir>` binary)
payload.body:
The sender, wire, and devcert code live under server/internal, so no other module can import them. Depending on the packaging question:
- **Go library:** move them to public packages (e.g. `http4/server/http4`) with a stable API, e.g. `http4.Handler(assets fs.FS, opts)` mountable on any webtransport-go server, or `http4.ListenAndServe(addr, tlsConfig, fs.FS)`.
- **Standalone binary:** `http4d serve ./site` serves a static site's pages over HTTPS (HTTP/1.1/2, plus Alt-Svc for h3) and its assets over HTTP4, with a real certificate (see the deployment issue) or the dev hash for localhost.

Acceptance: a separate example module (outside server/) imports the public package, or runs the binary, and serves the fixture pool, and the integrity suite passes against it.

payload.title: Integration layer: route a site's subresource loads over HTTP4 in the chosen integration style
payload.body: Implement whichever style the integration question picks, on top of the client library: - **Transparent Service Worker:** the site adds one script tag (and serves one sw.js). The worker intercepts same-origin subresource requests (img, link, script, fetch()) and answers them over an HTTP4 session, falling back to the network on any failure. Open risks, to check with a spike first: whether Chrome exposes WebTransport inside ServiceWorkerGlobalScope and how long a session survives worker termination; the first visit before the worker controls the page; and reusing one session across tabs. - **Explicit API:** the site calls `http4.fetch()` itself, and there are helpers for images (blob URLs) and styles. - **Declarative:** attributes such as `` / ``, rewritten by a loader script. CSS-referenced resources (fonts, background images) are not covered. Acceptance: an unmodified sample site (plain HTML/CSS/JS/images, apart from the integration's documented one-time setup) loads all same-origin subresources over HTTP4 in Chrome, verified by the library's per-request transport report, and loads correctly with HTTP4 disabled.

payload.title: Deployable demo: trusted TLS certificate, UDP/443 reachability, and hosting for a public HTTP4 site
payload.body:
Everything so far relies on serverCertificateHashes, a localhost dev mechanism that requires certificates valid for under 14 days and a hash delivered out of band. A public demo needs:
- A CA-trusted certificate (e.g. ACME/Let's Encrypt) for the site's hostname, used by both the page server and the WebTransport endpoint, with no hash pinning.
- A host where inbound UDP (ideally 443) reaches the server. Many PaaS and CDN front ends only proxy TCP HTTP, so the demo may need a VM or a UDP-capable load balancer.
- Documented fallback when UDP is blocked on the visitor's side (corporate networks). The client library's fallback covers this; the demo should show it.

Acceptance: the demo loads over HTTP4 from a real hostname in a stock Chrome with no flags, and falls back cleanly with UDP blocked.

payload.title: Demo site: a small real-looking site built only on the HTTP4 libraries, with a live HTTP4-vs-HTTP/3 toggle and protocol stats
payload.body:
A sample site (e.g. an image gallery or article page: HTML, a layout-blocking stylesheet, a JS bundle, a web font, a dozen large images, and a few JSON API calls) that uses only the libraries' public APIs and documented setup. The demo shows:
- A toggle to load the same page over HTTP4 or over plain HTTP/3 (or HTTP/2 fallback).
- A live panel with per-resource transport, completion order and times (SRPT should visibly finish small and critical resources first), grants in flight, resends, and srtt.
- A page-load version of G4: first render and stylesheet timing with the big images present, HTTP4 vs HTTP/3.

Measures G7: % of same-origin subresource bytes served over HTTP4 (target 100 on Chrome). The site's source contains no protocol code; check with a grep for wire/transport imports outside the library entry.

Acceptance: a headless test loads the demo, reads the transport report, and records G7. `npm run demo` does not start a long-lived dev server by default; the user runs the demo server themselves.

payload.title: How should a site adopt the HTTP4 client library: transparent Service Worker, explicit JS API, or declarative HTML attributes?
payload.body: This decides how 'drop-in' G7 is and what the integration layer (iss-s05bzsh) builds. All three sit on the same client library (iss-61wbbxy), which falls back to normal fetch when WebTransport or UDP is unavailable.

options.option: Transparent Service Worker (recommended)
options.consequence: Truest drop-in: add one script tag + sw.js and every same-origin img/css/js/font/fetch() is routed over HTTP4 with no markup changes. Risks needing a spike first: WebTransport availability and session lifetime inside a Service Worker in Chrome; the first visit isn't controlled until the worker installs (clients.claim / reload); one session per worker shared by tabs.

options.option: Explicit JS API
options.consequence: Simplest and most predictable: the site calls http4.fetch() (and image/style helpers) where it wants HTTP4. Works immediately, but markup-referenced assets (img src, link href, CSS url()) need code changes, so it's less 'drop-in'.

options.option: Declarative attributes
options.consequence: No Service Worker: a loader script upgrades , , etc. Needs markup edits, and can't cover resources referenced from CSS (fonts, background images) or by the browser's preload scanner.

options.option: Service Worker + explicit API
options.consequence: Build the API first (useful on its own and for the benchmarks), then the Service Worker on top as the zero-change path. More work, but the demo can show both.

payload.title: How should the server side be packaged for sites: a Go library to embed, a standalone `http4d serve <dir>` binary, or both?
payload.body: Decides the public shape of server packaging (iss-e1fks2p). The sender currently lives in server/internal and can't be imported by other modules.

options.option: Standalone binary (recommended for the demo)
options.consequence: `http4d serve ./site` serves pages over HTTPS and assets over HTTP4 in one process. No Go code is needed to make a demo site; the least API to stabilise.

options.option: Go library
options.consequence: Public package (e.g. http4.Handler(fs.FS)) mountable in an existing Go/webtransport-go server. Most flexible for Go shops, but the API surface needs designing and versioning, and non-Go sites can't use it directly.

options.option: Both
options.consequence: Library first with the binary as a thin wrapper. The best end state, and a little more work up front.

payload.title: WebTransport is exposed to Service Workers: both the W3C spec and Chromium's IDL declare it [Exposed=(Window,Worker)]
payload.body: The W3C WebTransport spec IDL is `[Exposed=(Window,Worker), SecureContext] interface WebTransport`, and Chromium's third_party/blink/renderer/modules/webtransport/web_transport.idl (HEAD, read 2026-09-22) has the same attribute. In Web IDL, `Worker` covers every worker global scope, including ServiceWorkerGlobalScope. Neither the spec nor MDN mentions Service Workers specifically (MDN only says "available in Web Workers"), so the empirical check in fnd for the Chrome 153 spike is what confirms it in practice. Other browsers were not checked.

sources.note: WebTransport interface IDL: [Exposed=(Window,Worker), SecureContext]
Chromium IDL lines 8-10: Exposed=(Window,Worker), SecureContext
Only states availability in Web Workers; silent on Service Workers

payload.title: In Chrome 153 a Service Worker can open a WebTransport session (with serverCertificateHashes) and serve a page's img, stylesheet, module script and fetch() over HTTP4
payload.body:
Spike, 2026-09-22: Chrome 153.0.8010.53 headless on macOS arm64, against http4d on loopback. The Service Worker bundles client/src/transport.ts, connects with serverCertificateHashes (typeof WebTransport in the SW is "function"; connect took 4.6 ms) and answers same-origin /assets/* fetch events with `new Response(bytes, {headers})` built from Http4Client.fetch(). The assets were deliberately absent from the HTTP server, so anything that loaded came over HTTP4.

Results: a 64×48 PNG decoded; the stylesheet applied (computed background rgb(1, 2, 3)); an ES module script executed; fetch() of JSON returned the body with the x-served-by: http4 header; 3 MB arrived in 38 ms. Server: 9 RPCs, 3,000,474 data bytes, 0 un-granted bytes.

Not yet tested: Firefox/Safari, many tabs sharing one worker, navigation requests, Range requests (media), the Cache API.

sources.note: Spike code: session scratchpad sw-spike/ (sw-src.js, www/index.html, run.ts). Re-creatable from this description; not committed.

payload.title: Chrome terminates an idle Service Worker after ~30 s even with an open WebTransport session; the session dies with it and the next request pays for a restart plus a reconnect
payload.body:
Probe without DevTools attached (plain `--headless=new`, results logged to the console, so Playwright's DevTools attachment couldn't keep the worker alive), Chrome 153, 2026-09-22. After an uninterrupted 45 s idle gap, and again after 75 s, the worker's startup timestamp had changed, meaning it was terminated and restarted. The next fetch still succeeded over HTTP4 in 10–13 ms on loopback, against 2–7 ms warm, because the new worker instance reconnected. A forced stop (CDP ServiceWorker.stopAllWorkers) behaved the same: the next request took 7 ms, with a reconnect of 2.7 ms. Earlier runs under Playwright showed no termination after 45 s, which is consistent with DevTools keeping workers alive, so tests must not rely on that.

Implications: on a real path every idle restart costs ≥2 RTTs (QUIC handshake + WebTransport CONNECT), plus the config fetch unless it is cached. The restart also discards srtt, grant state, and in-flight transfers. A session owned by the page or a SharedWorker (the Service Worker only intercepts and forwards over postMessage) would live as long as the tab instead.

sources.note: Spike sw-spike/www/idle.html run in plain headless Chrome: 'worker restarted during 45s gap: true', 'during 75s gap: true'

payload.title: A Service Worker does not see the first visit's subresources: resources in the initial HTML are requested before the worker controls the page
payload.body: Spike, Chrome 153: on the first load, an in the initial HTML went to the network (404, naturalWidth 0), even though the worker calls skipWaiting() + clients.claim(). The page is only claimed after activation, by which time the parser has already requested the image. After a reload, the same was served over HTTP4 (naturalWidth 64). A drop-in Service Worker integration therefore needs a fallback so first-visit resources load normally, and either accepts that the first visit isn't HTTP4 or triggers a one-time reload.

payload.title: Chrome rejects an HTTP4-served module script that has no Content-Type (strict MIME checking), so HTTP4 must carry response metadata

Strict MIME type checking is enforced for module scripts per HTML spec." The same bytes with Content-Type text/javascript executed. This confirms iss-tj4v2z2: the protocol has to deliver Content-Type (extension guessing in the worker would work for the spike, but not for extensionless routes).

This decides how 'drop-in' G7 is and what the integration layer (iss-s05bzsh) builds. All the options sit on the same client library (iss-61wbbxy), which falls back to normal fetch when WebTransport or UDP is unavailable.

Research 2026-09-22 (findings fnd-ph2znj3, fnd-q99xxg1, fnd-f844ews, fnd-hnymjv8, fnd-7ecs69k):
- **Feasible:** Chrome 153 exposes WebTransport in Service Workers, and a worker served an img, a stylesheet, a module script and fetch() over HTTP4.

options.option: Transparent Service Worker, SW owns the session
options.consequence: Simplest SW design: one script tag + sw.js, no markup changes. Proven feasible in Chrome 153. Cost: after each ~30 s idle period the worker is killed and the session with it, so the next load pays ≥2 RTT to reconnect and loses RTT/grant state. The first visit isn't HTTP4.

It avoids the reconnect-after-idle cost and keeps srtt and grant state warm, and it is still zero markup changes. The page must be open to serve, so it falls back to the network when there's no controlling client with a session. A bit more plumbing, plus a transfer of the body bytes from page to SW.

options.option: Explicit JS API
options.consequence: Simplest and most predictable: the site calls http4.fetch() (and image/style helpers) where it wants HTTP4, and the session lives in the page. Markup-referenced assets (img src, link href, CSS url()) need code changes, so it's less 'drop-in'.

options.option: Declarative attributes
options.consequence: No Service Worker: a loader script upgrades , , etc. Needs markup edits, and can't cover resources referenced from CSS (fonts, background images) or by the preload scanner.

options.option: Service Worker + explicit API
options.consequence: Build the explicit API first (useful on its own and for the benchmarks), then a Service Worker on top as the zero-change path. The demo can show both.

payload.title: Client integration: explicit JS API with a page-owned HTTP4 session, plus a Service Worker that forwards intercepted subresource requests to that session and falls back to the network
payload.body:
Chosen by the user on 2026-09-22 (option 5 built as option 2).

Layers:
1. **Explicit API.** `http4.fetch()` returns a Response. The HTTP4 session lives in the page (built in iss-61wbbxy). It is usable on its own and by the benchmarks.
2. **Service Worker on top.** It intercepts same-origin subresource requests (img, link, script, fetch()) and forwards each to the requesting tab's session. `FetchEvent.clientId` picks the tab, a postMessage/MessageChannel carries the request, and the body comes back as a transferred ArrayBuffer (no copy). Every tab serves its own requests. Markup is unchanged: the site adds a script tag and sw.js.
3. **Fallback.** Navigations, first-visit resources (fnd-hnymjv8), requests arriving before the page session is ready (or after a short wait), and any HTTP4 failure go to the network. A Service Worker-owned session (option 1) can be added later as an optional fallback, not the main path.

Why: the Service Worker makes it drop-in (no markup changes). The page-owned session lives as long as the tab, which avoids the reconnect after the ~30 s idle termination (fnd-f844ews), and srtt and grant state stay warm. The explicit API comes for free because it is the layer everything else is built on.

Rejected:
- Service Worker-owned session as the main path: pays ≥2 RTT and loses state after every idle kill.
- Explicit API only: markup-referenced assets need code changes.
- Declarative attributes: need markup edits and can't reach CSS-referenced resources.

Open risk, to verify first in iss-s05bzsh: forwarding requests from the Service Worker to the page (MessageChannel round trip, latency and transfer of large bodies) is untested. The spike (fnd-q99xxg1) proved only WebTransport and Response construction inside the Service Worker. Response metadata (iss-tj4v2z2) is a prerequisite: fnd-7ecs69k shows Chrome refuses module scripts without Content-Type.

patch.title: Integration layer: Service Worker that forwards a site's subresource requests to the page-owned HTTP4 session, with network fallback
patch.body:
Implements dec-sf6t0g6 on top of the client library (iss-61wbbxy), which provides the explicit API and the page-owned session.

**Step 1: verify the one unproven piece first.** Forward requests from the Service Worker to the page. - **Fallback to network:** no controlling client, the client has no session yet (after a short bounded wait), the session failed, or an HTTP4 ERROR. First-visit resources (fnd-hnymjv8) take this path.
- **Metadata:** Responses carry the server's Content-Type etc. (iss-tj4v2z2; fnd-7ecs69k shows it's mandatory).

payload.title: Response metadata is a separate META packet (0x06): a 4-name allowlist, printable-ASCII values, a 512-byte server budget, no grant needed; a transfer completes only with body + META
payload.body:
Implemented in iss-tj4v2z2 (option 2 of that issue); wire format v1.

The design:
- **Fields:** content-type, etag, last-modified and cache-control, in that order on the wire, at most 4. There is deliberately no content-encoding, because bodies are raw bytes.
- **Values:** 1–65535 bytes of printable ASCII with no leading or trailing space. The decoder rejects unknown, differently-cased or duplicate names.
- **Size:** the server keeps META within 512 bytes, dropping cache-control, then last-modified, then etag rather than exceed that.
- **Sending:** META goes out immediately before packet 0, and again for a repeated REQ. It is metadata, not body, so it needs no grant and never counts toward G2.
- **Completion:** the client completes a transfer only when it has both the full body and META. Missing META is recovered by repeating the REQ.
- **ETag:** a strong validator, the first 16 hex digits of the body's SHA-256.
- **Error statuses:** httpStatusFor maps NOT_FOUND → 404, BAD_REQUEST → 400, UNKNOWN_RPC → 503 (state was dropped, so a retry can succeed), and anything else → 502.

Rejected:
- A metadata block inside packet 0: it complicates offsets.
- Guessing the type from the file extension on the client: it's wrong for extensionless routes.

payload.title: Network impairment is a user-space UDP proxy (server/cmd/impair) plus http4d -advertise-wt; the proxy spins for the last 2 ms before each delivery
payload.body:
Implemented in iss-x4fs0fm.

The proxy is a NAT-style UDP forwarder, with each direction impaired separately: delay, jitter, optional reordering, random loss, Gilbert-Elliott burst loss, and a rate cap with a tail-dropping queue. Everything random is seeded. http4d -advertise-wt points config.json at the proxy without moving the listener. The test harness takes an opt-in `impair` option and reserves a free UDP port first, because http4d has to advertise the proxy's address before the proxy starts.

The delivery goroutine sleeps on a timer until 2 ms before a packet is due, then spins. macOS timers wake ~1.2 ms late per hop, which put a 50 ms RTT at ~52.5–53 ms and broke the ±2 ms precision requirement. The cost is some CPU while a packet is imminent.

Rejected: dummynet/pfctl or tc, which need root, differ by OS, and can't run inside a one-shot test.

payload.title: At 50 ms RTT the client's throughput is capped by its fixed 128 KiB grant budget (~2.2 MB/s measured vs a ~2.6 MB/s ceiling), and 1% loss stretches a 2 MB transfer from 0.94 s to 3.7–7.1 s
payload.body:
tests/impair (Chrome 153, loopback through the impairment proxy), 2026-09-22.

| Condition | srtt | 4 KiB api.json | 150 KB | 2 MB single | 2 MB concurrent | Recovery |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 50 ms RTT, no loss | 50.9 ms | 102 ms (2 RTT) | 208 ms | 942 ms | 1021 ms | none |
| 50 ms RTT, 1% loss each way | 51.8 ms | 103 ms | 336 ms | 3.7 s | 7.1 s | 16 recoveries, 49 RESENDs, 507 KB duplicate bytes |

In the lossy run the proxy dropped 41 of 4,341 packets downstream and 8 of 1,009 upstream.

Interpretation:
- **Throughput cap:** 128 KiB ÷ 50 ms ≈ 2.6 MB/s, and 2 MB at ~0.94 s is ≈2.2 MB/s, so the budget is the bottleneck. This is iss-66pc8rp.
- **Loss:** each stall costs one RTO while holes fill the budget, and timeout-driven recovery re-requests delayed-but-not-lost data (the duplicate bytes). This is iss-e58kfkh.

payload.title: The client's 4-packet initial grant is sized from Chrome's send limit (4 × 1007 = 4028 B), so a 4 KiB API response needs 2 RTTs instead of 1
payload.body: In tests/impair at 50 ms RTT, api.json (4096 B) took 102 ms, i.e. 2 RTTs. Http4Client sets initialGrant = 4 × maxPayload(wt.datagrams.maxDatagramSize) = 4 × 1007 = 4028 bytes. But maxDatagramSize limits only what the browser sends (fnd-ewhfy4b), and the server sends 1183-byte payloads. The initial grant therefore falls 68 bytes short of a 4 KiB response, and the rest waits for a GRANT round trip. That directly hurts G3, whose workload is ≤4 KiB API responses. Fix: size the initial grant in bytes to cover the target response size (e.g. ≥4096, or about one BDP per iss-66pc8rp), independent of the browser's send limit.

payload.title: HTTP/3 baseline is served at /h3/ on the WebTransport QUIC listener itself, and the bench throws on any baseline request that isn't h3
payload.body:
Implemented in iss-0sjtwnx.
- **Same listener:** /h3/<asset-id> sits on the same http3 mux as /wt and /echo. Both stacks share the UDP port, certificate, quic-go config and congestion controller, and behind the impairment proxy they cross the same impaired path.
- **Headers:** CORS and Timing-Allow-Origin go only to the page's loopback origin, and Cache-Control: no-store keeps every fetch off the browser cache.
- **Browser setup:** Chrome is launched with --origin-to-force-quic-on=<advertised WT host:port> and --ignore-certificate-errors-spki-list=<SPKI SHA-256>, exposed in config.json and the ready line.
- **Enforcement:** the bench page (client/bench, window.__bench.run(schedule)) throws if any h3 result's nextHopProtocol isn't "h3". Each request gets a unique URL so its Resource Timing entry is unambiguous.

Rejected: a separate h3 port. It would need its own proxy path and would let the two stacks see different network conditions.

payload.title: Client library contract: connect() never rejects; the report distinguishes http4/fallback/platform; NOT_FOUND is a final 404; /assets/<id> maps to asset <id>
payload.body:
Implemented in iss-61wbbxy (client/src/index.ts, bundled to client/dist/http4.js).
- **connect():** always resolves. It either has an HTTP4 session, or is fallback-only after a 5 s timeout, missing WebTransport, or a failed connect, with unavailableReason set.
- **Report transports:** "http4" (served by HTTP4), "fallback" (eligible for HTTP4 but served by the platform fetch after a failure), and "platform" (never eligible: cross-origin, non-GET/HEAD, a body, Range, or a non-asset path). G7 is measured over the eligible requests (http4 + fallback).
- **Errors:** NOT_FOUND over HTTP4 returns a 404 without retrying over HTTP. Every other HTTP4 failure falls back to the platform fetch.
- **Mapping:** the default is same-origin /assets/<id> ↔ asset ID <id>, and http4d serves the same pool over HTTP at that prefix (-asset-prefix), with the same Content-Type and ETag as META.
- **Limits:** Range requests always use the platform fetch, because HTTP4 has no ranges. HEAD transfers and discards the body for now.

payload.title: At 50 ms RTT, warm HTTP/3 fetches the 8-asset batch (~2.2 MB) in ~76 ms vs ~1017 ms for HTTP4 (≈13× slower); on clean loopback they are comparable (~17 vs ~21 ms)

tests/h3 (Chrome 153), 2026-09-22, concurrent PAGE_ASSETS batch (0 B to 2 MB), median of 5 runs. Clean loopback: h3 16.6–18.8 ms, HTTP4 20.5–23.1 ms. Through the proxy at 50 ms RTT: h3 75.7–77.6 ms (individual runs 73–108), HTTP4 1017–1018 ms (1014–1056).

payload.title: Fix the race between webtransport-go Server.Serve and Close when http4d is closed right after Start
payload.body: Found by the race detector in iss-61wbbxy. server.Start launches `go s.wtSrv.Serve(udpConn)`. payload.body: Found in iss-61wbbxy. Once the WebTransport session ends (server restart, network change, idle close), the Http4 handle stays fallback-only for the rest of the page's life. The page-owned session in dec-sf6t0g6 is meant to live as long as the tab, so it needs to reconnect: on session close, retry connect with exponential backoff (plus jitter), falling back for requests in the meantime. payload.body: Found in iss-61wbbxy. The library's HEAD currently fetches the full body over HTTP4 and discards it. A HEAD could send REQ with initial_grant = 0, resolve once META and the empty packet 0 (total_size → Content-Length) arrive, and then abandon the RPC. The server would evict it on idle. The client needs a request mode that completes without the body. Low priority.

Both matter for real pages. The first page load is cold for both stacks, and subsequent loads are warm. Add to the bench harness a way to start each run on a fresh QUIC connection for both stacks (new browser context, or closing and reopening the WebTransport session and forcing a new h3 connection), and report cold and warm results separately in the G3/G4 benchmarks.

payload.title: Grant budget = clamp(2 × maxRate × minRtt, 128 KiB, 16 MiB); initial_grant ≈ one BDP within 4–64 KiB (≥ 4096 B); pre-sample RTO backs off; GRANT probes feed minRtt only
payload.body:
Implemented in iss-66pc8rp (client/src/budget.ts).
- **Rate estimate:** a windowed max of delivery-rate samples over 10 delivery rounds (rounds, not wall time, so it survives idle gaps), with one sample per max(4 ms, minRtt) interval. Samples from intervals where the budget wasn't the limit count only if they raise the max.
- **RTT:** minRtt over 10 s. The min is used, not srtt, because queueing inflates srtt exactly when the pipe is full.
- **Growth and backoff:** growth comes implicitly from k = 2 (roughly doubling per RTT while the budget is the limit) and settles when QUIC's congestion window levels off, so QUIC stays in charge of congestion control. Each loss recovery shrinks the budget ×0.85 and blocks growth for one minRtt.
- **Bounds and queue:** the floor is 128 KiB (the old fixed budget), so short paths don't regress. The cap is 16 MiB, and incomingHighWaterMark follows the budget.
- **Initial grant:** about one BDP, clamped to 4–64 KiB and to the free budget, and exactly 4096 bytes before any estimate. It is sized in bytes, fixing fnd-kaff3cj.
- **Before the first RTT sample:** timeouts back off (RFC 6298 §5.5, 100 ms → at most 1 s, once per timeout period). Time from a GRANT to its first newly-allowed byte is used as a minRtt probe only, never for srtt, and the RTO falls back to 3 × minRtt until a clean REQ sample exists.

payload.title: At 150 ms RTT the client never got an RTT sample: the fixed 100 ms pre-sample RTO fired before every REQ's reply, and Karn's rule discarded every sample
payload.body: Found in iss-66pc8rp. Fixed by backing off the pre-sample RTO (RFC 6298 §5.5, up to 1 s). payload.title: Profile the multi-asset batch gap vs HTTP/3 (HTTP4 1.55–1.8× slower on the 8-asset batch) before the G3 benchmark
payload.body:

payload.title: Service Worker integration: the worker holds no session; it forwards subresources to the requesting tab over a MessageChannel; one classic-script tag /http4/auto.js first in <head>
payload.body:
Implemented in iss-s05bzsh, following dec-sf6t0g6.
- **Worker (/http4-sw.js):** it holds no HTTP4 session and uses skipWaiting + clients.claim. It leaves to the network: navigations, non-GET/HEAD, cross-origin, Range, requests with no clientId, and the bootstrap paths (/http4/*, /http4-sw.js, /config.json). Everything else is forwarded to the requesting tab.
- **Protocol:**
  1. On first contact with a tab, the worker sends hello with a MessagePort. The tab answers connecting, then ready {available, reason, assetPrefix}.
  2. For each request, the worker sends serve {url, method}. The tab answers {transport: "http4", status, headers, body} with the ArrayBuffer transferred, or fallback/platform with a reason.
  3. report returns the log for one tab or all tabs.
- **Falls back to the network when:** there's no hello ack within 500 ms, the tab isn't ready within 2 s, the session is unavailable, the page answers fallback, or a 1 s watchdog finds the tab closed.
- **Setup:** `<script src="/http4/auto.js"></script>`, a classic IIFE placed first in <head> so it runs before the parser requests the rest. It calls install() (session, worker registration, startMessages()), only accepts messages from our worker's scriptURL, and exposes window.http4 = {ready, registration, controlled, report({all?})}. data-config-url and data-asset-prefix are optional.
- **Library:** connect() now honours config.json's assetPrefix and reads it even without WebTransport, so fallback-only tabs classify requests correctly.
- **Report entries:** {url, method, destination, transport, reason?, status, ms, bytes, clientId}, capped at 2000, kept in worker memory.

Consequences: G7 must count only transferred bytes, measured loads disable the cache via CDP, and sites currently can't control reload caching of HTTP4 responses explicitly.

The session is page-owned (dec-sf6t0g6), so every navigation opens a new WebTransport session: a QUIC handshake + CONNECT, then META/packet 0 with a pre-sample RTO, then a budget ramp from the 128 KiB floor. - **Carry estimates across navigations:** keep minRtt, maxRate and budget in sessionStorage so a new session starts with a warm budget and RTO (still paying the handshake).

Revalidation over HTTP4 (If-None-Match → a 304-equivalent) doesn't exist yet. Decide whether `no-cache` should mean a full HTTP4 re-fetch, or whether to add a conditional REQ.

payload.body:
Implemented in iss-e58kfkh (RepairTracker in client/src/reassembly.ts, used by transport.ts).
- **Suspect:** a gap is a suspect once the transfer's frontier is more than 3 server packets past it. The allowance drops to 0 once the frontier reaches the grant, since no later data will reveal it.
- **Lost:** a suspect is declared lost after staying missing for a RACK-style window of max(1 ms, minRtt / 4). The window doubles on each spurious repair, up to srtt.
- **Re-request hold:** a RESENT range isn't requested again for 1.5 RTT plus the time to drain the server's 32-datagram send queue at the measured rate.
- **Tail probe:** if a transfer's tail stalls for 2 srtt plus drain time, its last packet is re-requested once.
- **Stall timer:** it RESENDs only real gaps below the frontier plus first/last tail probes, never the whole outstanding range (fixes fnd-smjbr3p). Its timeout is at least the drain time of outstanding bytes (capped at 10 s), and it shares the tracker with early detection.
- **Budget:** early-detected loss doesn't shrink the budget at all, because QUIC's congestion control already reacts and the delivery-rate estimate falls on its own. Only a stall-timer recovery backs off, at most once per RTT. This addresses fnd-py45re8 / iss-jmmt83p.
- **Options:** earlyResend (default true) and reorderPackets are optional ClientOptions.

payload.title: At ≥1% loss or with heavy reordering through the proxy, plain HTTP/3 is as slow as HTTP4 (13–22 s for the 2.2 MB batch): QUIC's shared congestion control sets the pace, so absolute deadlines on 50 MiB may be infeasible for any QUIC stack
payload.body:
From iss-e58kfkh, full 8-asset batch through the proxy, median of 3, after early RESEND:

| Path | HTTP4 | h3 |
|---|---|---|
| ±10 ms jitter + reordering, no loss | 19.6 s | 21.8 s |
| 5% loss, 50 ms | 13.2 s | 13.0 s |
| 1% loss, 150 ms | 14.1 s | 17.4 s |

Matrix cell 1% × 50 ms, 10 MiB single: HTTP4 19.0 s (0.55 MB/s), h3 27.4 s (0.38 MB/s).

Both stacks run over the same quic-go connection type, and QUIC's loss-based congestion control (plus treating reordering as loss) caps throughput. The matrix's absolute per-cell deadlines (dec-1fv4z7v) therefore measure QUIC as much as HTTP4. A deadline relative to h3 on the same path (e.g. HTTP4 ≤ 1.5× h3) would test what HTTP4 controls.

On the smaller batch (no 2 MB image), HTTP4 is 1.5–1.6× slower than h3 at 1–5% loss. Per-transfer loss detection can't use other transfers' later packets to reveal a tail loss, while QUIC's packet numbers can.

payload.title: Session-wide loss detection: let any transfer's later packets reveal another transfer's tail loss (e.g. a per-session DATA sequence number, wire v2)
payload.body: From iss-e58kfkh. Loss detection is per transfer: a gap is found only when that transfer's own later bytes arrive past it, and a lost tail waits for a tail probe (2 srtt + drain). QUIC's packet numbers reveal any lost packet as soon as a later one arrives, regardless of stream. That's one reason HTTP4 is 1.5–1.6× slower than h3 on the small batch at 1–5% loss (fnd for the h3-parity finding). Option: the server stamps each DATA with a session-wide sequence number (a wire change, v2, with vectors and both codecs), and the client runs RACK across the session, so a missing sequence number followed by later ones marks exactly which (rpc, offset) was lost. Must keep G2 semantics and SRPT unchanged.

payload.title: Recovery polish: RTT for REQ retransmits when every first REQ is lost, and decay of the widened reordering window
payload.body:
From iss-e58kfkh.
1. **REQ retransmit timing:** when every first REQ is dropped (tests/loss 'client drops each first REQ'), there's still no srtt, so the REQ RTO stays at 100 ms and that scenario is timer-bound (127–138 ms). Use the GRANT-probe minRtt estimate (dec-550khn9) to time REQ retransmits once one exists.
2. **Window decay:** after spurious repairs double the RACK reordering window (up to srtt), it never shrinks. Decay it back toward minRtt / 4 over time without spurious repairs, as RACK-TLP does.

Low priority.

payload.title: The remaining failing matrix cells are bounded by QUIC's loss-based congestion control, not HTTP4: the standard steady-state model gives ≈0.3 MB/s at 1%×50 ms, below the ~0.7 MB/s the 50 MiB deadline needs
payload.body:
Estimate, not a measurement of quic-go's exact algorithm. The widely used steady-state model for loss-based congestion control is rate ≈ (MSS / RTT) × 1.22 / √p (Mathis et al.). With MSS ≈ 1200 B:
- 1% × 50 ms: 24 KB/s × 12.2 ≈ 0.29 MB/s
- 1% × 150 ms: ≈ 0.10 MB/s
- 5% × 50 ms: ≈ 0.13 MB/s

This matches the measurements. At 1% × 50 ms on 10 MiB, HTTP4 did 0.55 MB/s and h3 0.38 MB/s (fnd-e667gya). Full 2.2 MB batches take 13–17 s over both stacks at 1–5% loss.

The matrix deadline (dec-1fv4z7v) needs 50 MiB within 75 s at 1% × 50 ms, i.e. ~0.7 MB/s. That appears unreachable for any stack over this QUIC connection with random loss, which is why early RESEND (iss-e58kfkh) improved duplicates and small-object times but not the pass count. In the 1%×150 cell the budget sits at the 128 KiB floor because 2 × (delivery rate × minRtt) is below the floor at ~0.1 MB/s. That's the budget following the QUIC-limited rate, not the per-recovery collapse of fnd-py45re8.

payload.title: How should G5's matrix deadlines be defined, given that the lossy high-RTT cells look QUIC-bound for HTTP/3 too?
payload.body: G5 = % of the 9 loss × RTT cells where every fixture arrives intact (G1) with 0 un-granted bytes (G2) within a deadline. Two runs both give 55.6%. The four failing cells fail only on the absolute deadline for the 50 MiB fixture. Correctness and pacing hold everywhere. Plain HTTP/3 over the same QUIC connection is as slow or slower on those paths (fnd-e667gya), and the standard loss-based congestion model predicts ~0.1–0.3 MB/s there (fnd for the QUIC bound). So the absolute deadline mostly measures quic-go's congestion control, not HTTP4.

options.option: Relative deadline: HTTP4 must finish within k× HTTP/3 on the same path (e.g. k = 1.5) (recommended)
options.consequence: It measures what HTTP4 controls, and it's still strict. Each cell also runs the h3 baseline (the harness supports it), which roughly doubles matrix runtime. The lossy cells would likely pass today (HTTP4 was faster than h3 on 10 MiB at 1%×50).

options.option: Physics-based deadline from the congestion model (MSS/RTT × 1.22/√p, with a margin)
options.consequence: No h3 runs needed, but it relies on a simplified model of quic-go's congestion control, which may not match in every cell.

options.option: Keep absolute deadlines, but drop the 50 MiB fixture from lossy cells
options.consequence: Simple and fast, but ad hoc, and it tests less. Large-transfer behaviour under loss is no longer covered.

options.option: Keep G5 as is and try to beat QUIC's congestion control
options.consequence: It would need a different congestion controller on the server (e.g. BBR-style pacing, if quic-go supports it) or unreliable delivery without QUIC CC. That's a big research item and changes the proposal's 'on top of QUIC' premise.
